content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my petrol-powered lawn mower with a robotic mower controlled by an iPhone. You need to manually drive the machine around the perimeter of the yard once, and the system will build a virtual map. Once setup is complete, it will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be more convenient and easier to use for many people.

Automated camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my phone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three built-in cameras allow the mower to automatically map out the lawn area, with no need to bury underground boundary wires or install a separate RTK antenna.

The automated initial mapping process obviously takes considerably longer. But I think for people who are not very tech-savvy, this method may be simpler.

To test this idea, I had my mum, who lives out of state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any assistance from me throughout the process. She replied that everything worked fine. Honestly, I had originally been quite doubtful about whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot along the boundary and manually mark no-go zones.

The automated mapping did create one small quirk in my front yard. Because there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn within my map's coverage area.

I fixed the problem by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clearly visible dividing line between two lawns, extra care is needed during the initial mapping stage.

Seeing the world through the mower's cameras

The TerraMow's cameras also support one of my all-time favourite features. The iPhone app can show you in real time what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to open this feed in a larger window. I could sit indoors and watch from the mower's perspective as it made its way across the back yard.

This feature is not strictly necessary for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting, and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a similar camera feed feature.

The two iPhone apps are fairly similar in other respects. Both let you schedule work, adjust mowing modes, set zones, mark no-go areas, and remotely control the mower.

The TerraMow has one particularly well-designed feature in this last area. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should operate according to a schedule without any manual intervention. Still, the TerraMow's joystick is very handy for cleaning up missed patches.

Sometimes, it almost feels like controlling the robot with the power of thought (and it feels rather satisfying). I can hold the iPhone down at my side, and with just a slight movement of my thumb, the machine moves in the direction I want.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control method.

More aggressive mowing performance

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive to me than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and produced more noise while operating.

I would not say the TerraMow is loud, but the difference between the two is very noticeable. The Anthbot can run extremely quietly when operating, so much so that it is easy to forget it is still running even when it continues mowing after dark with its headlights on.

Because the TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation and needs daylight to operate reliably, it is more important to schedule it to mow during the day.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage with the product that covers the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow operates reliably and dependably. I relied on it for several weeks in a row and did not have to do any routine mowing myself at all.

When smart mapping becomes too clever

The visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up occasionally backfires.

The mower constantly adjusts the map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each mow takes some time, during which you cannot perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain in a row, I ran into an interesting edge case. Water pooled in part of the yard, and the TerraMow cleverly avoided that area on its next run.

The grass grew taller inside the circular area that was skipped. Over time, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches as things to keep avoiding, and even after the standing water had long dried up, that stretch of grass was never mowed again.

I used the remote control feature in the app to manually drive the mower over the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once that area returned to the look of a normal lawn, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Trimming the edges regularly also helps the TerraMow handle boundary areas more decisively. Tall grass growing along fuzzy boundaries might otherwise be misjudged as obstacles and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and relies more on boundaries and obstacles defined by the user. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac review

Having tried both systems, I lean towards recommending TerraMow's camera approach for most people.

For me, underground boundary wires were never on the table to begin with, and installing an RTK base station means having one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, hard-to-see boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook tall weeds for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In exchange, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable and dependable automatic mowing, an engaging live camera feed, and the best manual control experience in a robotic mower app that I have seen.

I actually enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. After handing this task over to a robot, I can devote more time to landscaping, trimming edges, and detailed tidying, while still keeping the lawn neat and attractive.

The TerraMow V1000 excels in this regard, enough for me to recommend it, especially for people who want a robotic mower but do not want to dig trenches to bury wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk around the entire yard boundary holding a phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and the official website, priced at US$999 after applying a US$200 coupon. You can also purchase it through the TerraMow official website.
